{{Short description|Distribution result for probability mathematics}}
[[File:Wiener process and its reflection upon reaching a crossing point.png|thumb|Simulation of Wiener process (black curve). When the process reaches the crossing point at ''a''=50 at ''t''<math>\approx</math>3000, both the original process and its reflection (red curve) about the ''a''=50 line (blue line) are shown. After the crossing point, both black and red curves have the same distribution.]]

In the theory of [[probability theory|probability]] for [[stochastic process]]es, the '''reflection principle''' for a [[Wiener process]] states that if the path of a Wiener process ''f''(''t'')  reaches a value ''f''(''s'') = ''a'' at time ''t'' = ''s'',  then the subsequent path after time ''s'' has the same distribution as the reflection of the subsequent path about the value ''a''.<ref name=Jacobs>{{cite book|last=Jacobs|first=Kurt|title=Stochastic Processes for Physicists|year=2010|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781139486798|pages=57–59|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bx8yN2IfE8kC&q=reflection+principle+wiener+process&pg=PA57}}</ref> More formally, the reflection principle refers to a [[theorem]] concerning the distribution of the supremum of the Wiener process, or Brownian motion. The result relates the distribution of the supremum of Brownian motion up to time ''t'' to the distribution of the process at time ''t''. It is a corollary of the [[strong Markov property]] of Brownian motion.

==Statement==
If <math> (W(t): t \geq 0) </math> is a Wiener process, and <math>a > 0</math> is a threshold (also called a crossing point), then the theorem states:
:<math> \mathbb{P} \left(\sup_{0 \leq s \leq t} W(s) \geq a \right) = 2\mathbb{P}(W(t) \geq a) </math>

Assuming <math> W(0) = 0 </math> , due to the continuity of Wiener processes, each path (one sampled realization) of Wiener process on <math> (0,t) </math> which finishes at or above value/level/threshold/crossing point <math>a</math> the time <math> t </math>  ( <math>W(t) \geq a</math> ) must have crossed (reached) a threshold <math>a</math> ( <math> W(t_a) = a </math> ) at some earlier time <math> t_a \leq t </math> for the first time . (It can cross level <math>a</math> multiple times on the interval <math>(0,t)</math>, we take the earliest.)

For every such path, you can define another path <math>W'(t)</math> on <math> (0,t) </math> that is reflected or vertically flipped on the sub-interval <math> (t_a,t) </math> symmetrically around level <math>a</math> from the original path. These reflected paths are also samples of the Wiener process reaching value <math> W'(t_a) = a </math> on the interval <math>(0,t)</math>, but finish below <math>a</math>. Thus, of all the paths that reach <math>a</math> on the interval <math> (0,t) </math>, half will finish below <math>a</math>, and half will finish above. Hence, the probability of finishing above <math>a</math> is half that of reaching <math>a</math>.
 
In a stronger form, the reflection principle says that if <math>\tau</math> is a [[stopping time]] then the reflection of the Wiener process starting at <math> \tau </math>, denoted <math> (W^\tau(t): t \geq 0)</math>, is also a  Wiener process, where:
:<math> W^\tau(t) = W(t)\chi_\left\{t \leq \tau\right\} + (2W(\tau) - W(t))\chi_\left\{t > \tau\right\}</math>
and the indicator function <math>\chi_{\{t \leq \tau\}}= \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if }t \leq \tau \\ 0, & \text{otherwise }\end{cases}</math> and <math>\chi_{\{t > \tau\}} </math> is defined similarly.  The stronger form implies the original theorem by choosing <math>\tau = \inf\left\{t \geq 0: W(t) = a\right\}</math>.

==Proof==
The earliest stopping time for reaching crossing point ''a'', <math> \tau_a := \inf\left\{t: W(t) = a\right\} </math>, is an almost surely bounded stopping time. Then we can apply the strong Markov property to deduce that a relative path subsequent to <math>\tau_a</math>, given by <math> X_t := W(t + \tau_a) - a </math>, is also simple Brownian motion independent of <math> \mathcal{F}^W_{\tau_a} </math>. Then the probability distribution for the last time <math>W(s)</math> is at or above the threshold <math>a</math> in the time interval <math>[0,t]</math> can be decomposed as
:<math> 
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a\right) & = \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a, W(t) \geq a\right) + \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a, W(t) < a\right)\\
& = \mathbb{P}\left(W(t) \geq a\right) + \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a, W(t) - W(\tau_a) < 0\right)\\
\end{align}</math>.

By the strong markov property, <math> W(t) - W(\tau_a) \overset{\mathcal{D}}{=} W'(t-\tau_a) </math> where <math> W'</math> is a second simple brownian motion independent of <math> \{W(u): 0 \leq u \leq \tau_a\} </math>.
Thus, by independence, the second term becomes:

:<math>
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a, W(t) - W(\tau_a) < 0\right) &= 
\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a, W'(t-\tau_a) < 0\right) \\
&=\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a\right) \mathbb{P}\left(W'(t-\tau_a) < 0\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a\right) ,
\end{align} 
</math>.
Since <math> W'(t) </math> is a standard Brownian motion independent of <math> \mathcal{F}^W_{\tau_a} </math> and has probability <math> 1/2 </math> of being less than <math>0</math>. The proof of the theorem is completed by substituting this into the second line of the first equation.<ref>Mörters, P.; Peres, Y. (2010) ''Brownian Motion'', CUP. {{isbn|978-0-521-76018-8}}</ref>

:<math> 
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a\right) & = \mathbb{P}\left(W(t) \geq a\right) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a\right) \\
\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}W(s) \geq a\right) &= 2 \mathbb{P}\left(W(t) \geq a\right)
\end{align}</math>.

==Consequences==
The reflection principle is often used to simplify distributional properties of Brownian motion. Considering Brownian motion on the restricted interval <math> (W(t): t \in [0,1]) </math> then the reflection principle allows us to prove that the location of the maxima <math> t_\text{max} </math>, satisfying <math> W(t_\text{max}) = \sup_{0 \leq s \leq 1}W(s) </math>, has the [[arcsine distribution]]. This is one of the [[Lévy arcsine law]]s.<ref name=Levy>{{cite journal|last=Lévy|first=Paul|title=Sur certains processus stochastiques homogènes|journal=Compositio Mathematica|year=1940|volume=7|pages=283–339|url=https://www.numdam.org/item?id=CM_1940__7__283_0|access-date=15 February 2013}}</ref>
